Title: AdapTools: Adaptive Tool-based Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic LLMs
Abstract: As open-source large language models (LLMs) become increasingly powerful, they are rapidly evolving into Agentic LLMs capable of automating complex daily tasks.However, this paradigm shift entails severe security risks, as the agents' necessary integration with external real-time data sources creates a direct pathway for indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks.Existing attack methods are limited by their reliance on static patterns and evaluation on simple language models, failing to address the fast-evolving nature of modern Agentic LLMs.We introduce Adap Tools, a novel adaptive IPI attack framework that selects stealthier attack tools and generates adaptive attack prompts to create a rigorous security evaluation environment.Our approach comprises two key components: (1) Adaptive Attack Strategy Construction, which develops transferable adversarial strategies for prompt optimization, and (2) Attack Enhancement, which identifies stealthy tools capable of circumventing task-relevance defenses.Comprehensive experiments on both open-source and commercial agentic LLMs show that Adap Tools achieves a per-model average improvement of 2.08× in attack success rate over the strongest baseline under state-ofthe-art defenses (MELON, Pi-Detector), with gains reaching up to 3.06× on the most resistant reasoning agents.The framework further transfers to black-box commercial agents (GPT, Qwen, Gemini), with ASR ranging from 4.2% to 20.3% (peak on the in-family Qwen-MAX), exposing systematic vulnerabilities in modern Agentic LLMs.llm agents.In Findings of the Association for Computational
Major_Contribution_Result: AdapTools is an adaptive indirect prompt injection framework that combines adaptive attack-strategy construction with attack enhancement (stealthy tool selection) against agentic LLMs. Authors report a per-model average 2.08× ASR improvement over the strongest baseline under MELON/Pi-Detector defenses (up to 3.06× on the most resistant reasoning agents), with transfer to black-box commercial agents at ASR ranging from 4.2% to 20.3% (peak on in-family Qwen-MAX). On open-source agents without defenses they report high ASRs (e.g., 60.6% Qwen-3-8B, 44.4% LLaMA-3.1-8B, 69.3% Mistral-8B).
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Authors state: attack synthesis depends on a capable attacker LLM (API cost/capability dependence); the Markov transition matrix is estimated from AgentAlign benign trajectories and may need re-estimation for different tool distributions; evaluation focuses on English ReAct text tool-calling agents (multi-modal/non-English/plan-and-execute left to future work); absolute ASR on top-tier commercial agents (GPT, Gemini) remains below 6%.
Critics: Useful as an adaptive red-team evaluation method against defended agentic LLMs, with explicit transfer results to commercial APIs. Numbers are attack-success oriented and defense-dependent; the paper does not provide a new general agent-security benchmark beyond its experimental suites. Absolute commercial ASRs are modest, so claims of systematic vulnerability should be read with those reported ranges.
